full_judgment:
3. The defendant No. 2 the Province of East Pakistan now Bangladesh filed written statement to contest the suit denying the material allegations in the plaint and contending inter-alia that the suit-land was first recorded in the name of defendant No. 2 but subsequently on the objection filed by the plaintiff the land of plot no. 1788/1583 was recorded in his name; that the plaintiff had knowledge of the record of right from the beginning; that the suit-land was in khas possession of the ex-rent receiver defendant No. 1 and the same now vested in the Government i.e. the contesting defendant No. 2 under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as excess Khas land of the ex-rent receiver; that the suit-land was delivered on temporary borga settlement with one Abdul Karim and Yar Baksh who have been possessing the same since the date of their borga settlement and they have applied for permanent lease of the suit land in respect of which Misc. Case Nos. 181/64-65 and 222/64-65 are pending. It has been further alleged that the plaintiff has no title or possession in the suitlands and hence he is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. The suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 11. Plaintiffs main case is that he took pattan (settlement) from the ex-landlord of the suit estate and on payment of rents he has been possessing the same after reclamation of the suit lands since 25/26 years back. To prove the case of his title, the plaintiff admittedly failed to produce any document save and except Ext. 1. He has stated that he has lost his dakhilas of payment of rents in respect of the suit-lands. He has submitted, of course one document namely Ext. 1 dated 5.7.53, a receipt of payment of rental of Rs. 11/4 annas to the Court of Wards which allegedly took over the administration of the same. According to the plaintiff, this is the only basic document to prove his title in the suit-lands. He has of course submitted some other documents namely Exts. 2 to 2(a). Exhibit 2 relates to an Advocate Commissioner's report in a proceeding in respect of Criminal Case No. 187 of 1943 of the Court of SDO Sunamganj between one Narendra Kumar Purakaysta as first party and Shamsher Ali and others as second party and Ext. 2(a) relates to a sketch map in respect of the same prepared by the said Advocate Commissioner, but there is nothing specific in these documents to show any connection with the suit-lands. Ext. 3 it appears to be a ceartified copy of an order dated 10.6.41 showing withdrawal of a case being-CR Case No. 575 of 1941 between one Naresh, Chandra Rai Vs. Shamsher under section 379 IPC and again this has-also no reference to the suit land. Ext. 4 another certified copy of judgment of another case being Cast No. 187 M/1943 between one Narendra Kumar Purakyastha Vs. Shamsher Ali and others under Section 147 CrPC dated 10.1.44. This appears to have also no reference to the suit-land but it has reference to a gopat. Ext. 5 is a certified copy of a plaint of Title Suit No. 19/65 between one Abdul Mannaf Vs. Shamser Ali and Ext. 6 appears to be a petition praying for an order of dismissal of the suit for non prosecution. This appears to have some reference with regard to possession over the suit-land but nothing about the title of the plaintiff over the same. All the above documents Exts. 2 to 6 have been filed by the plaintiff mainly in order to show his possession over the suit-lands. Exts. 3, 4 and 5 were admitted into evidence without objection but other documents namely Ext. 1, 2 to 2(i) and 6 were admitted into evidence after objection. The contesting defendant on the other hand filed Ext. A, a Fortified copy of the choice list and the list of excess khas land of the ex-landlord defendant No. 1 Dewan Obaidur Reza Chowdhury and Ext. B, is a certified copy of the khatian No. 49 not Paschim Haripur; Ext. C and C(1) are certified copies of Objection petition and the order sheet in Objection Case Nos. 18 of 1960 under section 19(1) of the EBS. A and Tenancy Act, filed by plaintiff Shamser Ali; Ext. D, D(1) are certified copies of the order sheet and the objection petition of plaintiff Sham= Ali under section 50 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in Miscellaneous Case No. 37/64; Ext. E is a carbon copy of order regarding possession of certain property in Proposal case No. 215 of 1960 and Ext. F is a certified copy of settlement map and Ext. G to G(2) for petitions of submission of rayati settlement proposal of the suit-lands by one Karim, Yar-Baksh and Abdun Nur. Of these documents. Ext. B, and Exts. C-C(1), D,D(1) series have been admitted into evidence without objection. But Ext. AEF-G-G(g) series appeared to have been admitted into evidence after objection. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record found possession of the suit-lands with the plaintiff, but with regard to the alleged documentary evidence Ext. I he has observed that the same does not show that the payment of rent was made in respect of the suit-lands He has also observed that the plaintiff has failed to prove a single dakhila of rent either to the landlord or to the Government acquired Estate and also there is no reasonable and satisfactory explanation as to the non-production of the alleged dakhilas. Now, the lower appellate Court appears to have believed this document Ext. I and found that payment of rent by this document was made against claim in Certificate Case No. 359 of the year 1952-1953. Now, I have to see how far the finding of the lower appellate Court is correct and sustainable in respect of the alleged title of the plaintiff in the suit-lands. So far the question of possession over the suit-lands, both the Courts below on consideration of the evidence on record, oral and documentary came to a concurrent finding in favour of the plaintiff. In the Second Appeal, I have no authority to disturb this concurrent finding of fact on possession unless it is found to be perverse or contrary to the evidence on record. Furthermore, inspite of the finding on possession by the trial Court in favour of the plaintiff the contesting defendant did not prefer any cross objection against such finding. So, I, have nothing to interfere with the same. 

 12. Now, I have to see only which court is correct in deciding the question of title of the plaintiff over the suit-lands. It is contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent that the contesting defendant has failed to prove its plea that the suit-property vested in the Government and the Government got khas possession of the same from the ex-rent-receiver. It appears that in order to prove vesting of the suit property in the Government the defendant has produced Ext. A a certified copy of the order-sheet of the vesting case along with the list of excess lands of the ex-rent-receiver and examined a Tahsildar of the Tashil office as DW 1 and no other document has been filed in the Court in proof of vesting. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate submits that the defendant has failed to prove the vesting of the suit property, particularly when the Gazettee Notification in this connection has not been filed by the contesting defendant. The learned Advocate for the appellant on the other hand submits that by a Gazettee Notification, the wholesale acquisition of the interest of all the rent receivers was made and the rent-receivers were asked to submit their lists of choice lands, but so far this suit-property is concerned, the ex-landlord did not make any choice as a result the same vested in the Government as excess land by operation of law. As regards the non production of the Gazettce notification, he however could not give satisfactory explanation. Be that as it may, whatsoever weakness there might be in the defendant's case, the plaintiff must prove his own case satisfactorily to obtain a decree. In that view of the matter, let. me see how far the plaintiff has been able to prove his title in the suit lands. Admittedly, the plaintiff could not file any document of tide save and except Ext. I, of course he has led some oral evidence also, but those relate to his possession and not to his alleged claim of title in the suit-lands. As regards his other documents, it has been observed by the Court of Appeal below to the effect that "Besides these, certified copies of the order-sheet, judgment and plaint of other criminal cases and title suits are filed but they will not be of much help to the plaintiff." In finding title in favour of the plaintiff, a presumption has been tried to be drawn by the lower appellate Court in favour of the plaintiff's alleged tenancy right in the suitlands for alleged non-production of some documents by the defendants alleged to have been called for by the plaintiff from them. 

 14. Now there is no denying of the fact that the plaintiff's success is dependant on the proof of genuineness of the document Ext I and its relation with the suit lands. On the face of it there is not specification or description of the land for which the alleged rent receipt was obtained. It appears that it was granted on behalf of the Court of Wards Estate by one Bhupesh Chandra Nag, but the plaintiff has neither examined that grantor Bhupesh Chandra nor he has given any explanation as to whether he was available in the country or not and why he has nt been produced in court as witness. Rather PW 2 says that the said Bhupesh is about 30/32 years who is alive. The document appears apparently to be related to the certificate case being No. 359/52-53, but the plaintiff has failed to bring any paper of such certificate case to show that the same related to the suit-lands. Besides from Ext I, it appears that the alleged payment of rent was made on behalf of Shamsher Ali by one Ainuddin of village Baishaber but that Ainuddin has not been produced. Similarly PW 3 says that one Janick Ali and Altafun assisted the plaintiff in reclaiming the suit land but they have also not been produced to support the plaintiffs case. Along with this, if we examine the document filed by the contesting defendant namely Exts C, C(1), D and D(1) which show that the plaintiff filed objection cases ups, 19(1) and 50 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the Revenue Authorities against recording of the names of the ex-rent-receiver in the settlement khatians but the said petitions were disallowed. It appears that Exhibits C and D series relate to objection cases of the years 1960 and 1964 relating to plot No. 1583 but strange enough this document Ext I allegedly a document of title of the plaintiff which is dated 5.7.53, was not produced before the revenue authority for correction of the record and instead in Objection case No. 18 of 1960 a RR of Rs. 2/8/ dated 27.5.62 was produced before the revenue authority as revealed by Ext C(1). This smacks of the concoction of the document Ext 1. Had it been a genuine document in possession of the plaintiff, certainly it would have been placed before the revenue authorities in the objection cases to prove his title in the suit lands and to get the record of right corrected in his name. So, the trial Court very correctly disbelieved the claim of title of the plaintiff. But the lower appellate court wrongly relied on the said document Ext I and illegally found title in favour of the plaintiff. In this connection the oral evidence of the parties may also be taken into consideration. PW 1 is the plaintiff. He himself at the very inception of his deposition stated that the disputed land was formerly khas patit of the ex-landlord Dewan Obaidur Reza. Then he said that he had taken pattan of 11 kedars of land some 25/26 years ago. He stated that he lost his dakhilas but this statement was not made in the plaint. He admitted that he has no papers to prove taking of pattan of the suit land from the ex-landlord. The other PWs namely PW 2-4 deposed only about possession of the plaintiff over the suit land and not about his claim of title by way of pattan. So, there is no evidence to corroborate PW I in his claim of title over the suit lands. On the contrary DW 1 has come to say that the suit property belonged to ex-rent-receiver defendant No. 1 which subsequently vested in the Government defendant No. 2. As to possession of the plaintiff, of course both the Cburts below on consideration of the evidence on record came to concurrent finding in his favour. But it is not the case of the plaintiff that he acquired title by way of adverse possession. He tried to base his claim of title on his alleged pattan which he ultimately failed to establish. Besides, it has not been contended on behalf of the plaintiff that he has fulfilled the basic requirements of any claim of title by adverse possession over the suit lands. Thus having regard to all aspects of the case and on careful and overall consideration of the entire evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the firm view that the plaintiff has totally failed to prove his right, title and interest in the suit land, though he has been found to be in possession of the same. For the reasons stated above, I therefore find that the impugned judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court can not be sustained in law and on facts and the same should be set aside.
